title: Indexes: why your query is slow
story:
Answering a question about one row, without help, means examining every row. That is tolerable in memory and intolerable against a device where each access costs a fixed and enormous delay regardless of how little you read — which is the constraint the storage lesson established and which this lesson is a direct response to.

Bayer and McCreight set out the response in 1972, and the framing in their opening is the whole design. They consider the organisation and maintenance of an index for a dynamic random access file, assuming the index must be kept on a backup store such as a disc. Assuming the index is on disc. Every property of the structure follows from that assumption rather than from abstract considerations about trees.

Their organisation allows retrieval, insertion and deletion of keys in time proportional to the logarithm of the index size, with the base being a device-dependent number, and storage utilisation of at least fifty percent. The phrase device-dependent is where the design lives. A binary tree would give you a logarithm base two, and against a disc that would be a disaster — every level is an access, and accesses are what you are trying to avoid. So the nodes are made wide instead: in a tree of order k each node holds at most 2k keys and 2k+1 pointers and at least k keys, so each node is at least half full. Size those nodes to the device's block and each access you pay for eliminates most of the remaining candidates rather than half of them.

That is the entire trick, and it is worth stating as a principle because it recurs: the structure is shaped by the cost of the medium rather than by elegance. Their experiments ran with indexes up to one hundred thousand keys, maintaining an index of fifteen thousand at an average of nine transactions per second on the hardware of the day — modest numbers that make the point, which is that the shape was chosen by measurement against real devices.

What it costs is the thing people forget when they add indexes freely. The structure has to be maintained, so every insert, update and delete now writes to the table and to every index over it. Reads get faster and writes get slower, storage grows, and an index nobody's queries use is pure cost. Which is why they are chosen deliberately rather than created by default — and why the first question about a slow query is not which index to add, but what the query is actually doing that requires examining rows it does not need.

problem.name: Indexed access
problem.shape: A question concerns a few rows and answering it without help means examining all of them, on a device charging a fixed cost per access.
tell: a query filters on a column and takes time proportional to the whole table
reads are fast and writes have become slow
indexes were added for every column somebody mentioned
a query plan shows a full scan where a lookup was expected
problem.move: Index the columns your queries actually filter and join on, sized and ordered to match those queries, and remove indexes nothing uses. Before adding one, read the plan — the answer is sometimes that the query is examining rows it does not need for a reason no index will fix.
problem.invariant: Each node is sized to the device's block so that one access eliminates most remaining candidates, giving a cost proportional to the logarithm of the index size in a base determined by the device rather than by the structure.
problem.breaks: Every index is maintained on every write, so reads get faster and writes get slower in proportion to how many you have. An index that no query uses is pure cost — storage, write amplification, and one more thing to keep consistent — and nothing in the system will tell you it is unused.

cost.time: slower inserts, updates and deletes, in proportion to the number of indexes
cost.space: a second structure alongside the data, at least half full by construction
cost.beats: scanning every row, which costs one access per block of the whole table, and keeping the table sorted, which makes every insert a rewrite

worked.problem: An index makes reads faster. What does it make slower, and why?
worked.reasoning:
Every write, and by an amount proportional to how many indexes exist — because an index is a second copy of part of the data that has to stay consistent with the first.

Start from what it is. An index is an ordered structure holding the indexed columns plus a reference back to the row. Ordered is the operative word: its usefulness comes entirely from the order, so any change to an indexed value must be reflected in the right place, not merely recorded.

So an insert writes the row and then inserts into every index over that table. A delete removes from all of them. An update touches every index whose columns it changed — and if it changes an indexed value, that is a removal from one position and an insertion at another, since the entry has to move to stay ordered. A table with five indexes turns one logical write into six physical ones.

There is a second cost specific to the structure. Nodes are kept at least half full, so an insertion into a full node splits it, and a split may propagate upward. Most inserts are cheap and occasional ones are much more expensive, which shows up as latency variance rather than as a higher average — and variance is harder to diagnose than a uniform slowdown.

The reason the structure is shaped this way at all is the device. The design assumes the index lives on a store where each access has a large fixed cost, so nodes are made wide and sized to the block: retrieval, insertion and deletion cost the logarithm of the index size in a base that is device-dependent rather than two. A binary tree would make every level a separate access, which is exactly what you were trying to avoid.

Two practical consequences I would give. An index that no query uses is pure cost — write amplification, storage, and another thing to keep consistent — and nothing in the system will tell you it is unused, so you have to go and look. And before adding one, read the query plan, because the answer is sometimes that the query is examining rows it does not need for a reason no index addresses: a function applied to the column that prevents the order being used, a predicate that matches most of the table, or a join whose direction makes the index inapplicable.

problem.practice: Take a slow query and read its plan before changing anything. Then list every index on the table it touches and work out which queries use each one — any index you cannot attribute to a query is costing you writes for nothing.

beats.broke: Answering a question about one row means examining every row, and the rows live on a device where each access costs a fixed and enormous delay regardless of how little you read.
beats.fix: Keep an ordered structure beside the data whose nodes are sized to the device's block, so each access eliminates most of the remaining candidates rather than one of them.
beats.cost: The structure is maintained on every write, so every index makes insertion, update and deletion slower and consumes storage — which is why they are chosen rather than created by default.

interview.q: An index makes reads faster. What does it make slower, and why?
interview.trap: Saying writes, and stopping. The mechanism matters: an indexed value that changes must move within the ordered structure, node splits make the cost uneven rather than uniformly higher, and an index no query uses still pays all of it.
